extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary essays; educated audience interested in rhetoric, style, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing personal essays and rhetorical prose (with parallel observations on conduct in love). Emphasises voice, conception, restraint, and natural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and opportunity in love
rubrics_metrics.description: “the first thing to be considered in love matters, I should answer that it was how to take a fitting time; and so the second; and so the third--‘tis a point that can do everything.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the right moment — timing can determine success in courtship or intrigue. Examples: making way for Maecenas (feigning sleep) to allow lovers' opportunity; failing to take or create opportunity is often the only obstacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve reverence in pursuit
rubrics_metrics.description: “he who in this traffic takes away the reverence, defaces at the same time the lustre.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain respect and avoid giving offence when pursuing someone; reverence enhances attraction. Anti-pattern: brutish or disrespectful behaviour that diminishes a beloved's allure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt humility and modest play in courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would in this affair have a man a little play the child, the timorous, and the servant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playfulness, modesty, and a degree of apparent timidity can be effective in wooing; theatrical humility can increase desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of modesty — avoid affected coyness
rubrics_metrics.description: “if it be not wholly simple or childish, ‘tis silly, and unbecoming ladies in this commerce, and presently runs into impudence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False or performative modesty is self-defeating; modesty must be genuine. Affected looks or cant that betray the tongue (eyes give the lie to the tongue) are ridiculed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obsessively investigate jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Curiosity is vicious throughout; but ‘tis pernicious here. ‘Tis folly to examine into a disease for which there is no physic…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching obsessively for proof of infidelity inflames the problem, often increases shame, and harms children/families; remedyless inquiries are injurious. Romans' custom of warning wives before return is cited as a preventive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint and delay heighten value
rubrics_metrics.description: “To stay its flight and delay it with preambles: all things -- a glance, a bow, a word, a sign, stand for favour and recompense betwixt them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaying gratification, valuing small tokens and preambles, and pacing pleasures intensifies desire — applicable to courtship and to pacing in art/writing (restraint increases worth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestiveness over explicitness in erotic description
rubrics_metrics.description: “Both the action and description should relish of theft.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evocative, suggestive description (implying more than is said) is preferable to blunt explicitness; modesty that forces guessing can be treacherous, but well-managed reserve arouses imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid conception produces language
rubrics_metrics.description: “This painting is not so much carried on by dexterity of hand as by having the object more vividly imprinted in the soul.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong, clear conception of the subject should drive expression; thought and imagery illuminate and generate fitting words. Anti-pattern: relying on verbal dexterity alone without vivid thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct, vigorous, and unified style
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nothing forced, nothing languishing, but everything keeps the same pace... 'tis nervous and solid, that does not so much please, as it fills and ravishes the greatest minds.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for energy, unity, and muscular expression rather than soft or languid eloquence. The best passages are direct, lively, and substantial rather than merely ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use language to serve conception; enrich words by use
rubrics_metrics.description: “They do not create words, but they enrich their own, and give them weight and signification by the uses they put them to, and teach them unwonted motions, but withal ingeniously and discreetly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective writers adapt and strain existing words to fit strong ideas instead of inventing empty neologisms. Practice varied and apt uses of familiar vocabulary to increase expressive power. Anti-pattern: adopting strange new words without clear meaning (Montaigne's criticism of contemporary French scribblers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and empty neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is nothing seen in their writings but a wretched affectation of a strange new style... provided they can but trick themselves out with new words, they care not what they signify.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty for its own sake (new words, odd constructions) that lacks substance weakens writing. Seek invention plus discretion; new forms must convey meaning and not merely decorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and consistent personal voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “I correct the faults of inadvertence, not those of custom... 'Tis enough that I have done what I designed; all the world knows me in my book, and my book in me.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the individuality of your voice and the idiosyncrasies that make the work yours; correct careless mistakes but don't neuter customary speech that constitutes authentic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish imitation and beaten arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: “I more unwillingly undertake beaten arguments, lest I should handle them at another’s expense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for originality; be wary of repeating others' familiar topics in a way that exposes you as derivative. When influenced, acknowledge and transform rather than simply mimic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical resources when native language flags
rubrics_metrics.description: “if you would maintain the dignity of your style, you will often perceive it to flag and languish under you, and there Latin steps in to its relief...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When native idiom lacks terms or vigor for a noble tone, borrow classical language, metaphors, or forms to sustain dignity and force; transplanting forms can strengthen expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let sense illuminate words; avoid empty rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: “the sense illuminates and produces the words, no more words of air, but of flesh and bone; they signify more than they say.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words must carry the weight of meaning grounded in perception and experience; aim for language that signifies richly rather than rhetorical flourishes that say little.
